entries.f5dcf8644adf18ee434c86456e1aef37bdcfeebb: <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.17">2Sa 14:17</reference> <hi type="italic">“Then thine handmaid thought, may the word of my lord the king be for rest </hi>(i.e., tend to give me rest);<hi type="italic">for as the angel of God </hi>(the angel of the covenant, the mediator of the blessings of divine grace to the covenant-nation), <hi type="italic">so is my lord the king to hear good and evil </hi>(i.e., listening to every just complaint on the part of his subjects, and granting help to the oppressed),<hi type="italic">and Jehovah thy God be with thee!”</hi>
entries.9985e0db57724fe053596de0b8b8a9422e1c2472: <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.18-2Sam.14.19">2Sa 14:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen4439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4440" type="x-p"/> These words of the woman were so well considered and so crafty, that the king could not fail to see both what she really meant, and also that she had not come with her petition of her own accord. He therefore told her to answer the question without disguise: whether the hand of Joab was with her in all this. She replied,<hi type="italic">“Truly there is not </hi>(אם) <hi type="italic">anything to the right hand or to the left of all that my lord the king saith,”</hi> i.e., the king always hits the right point in everything that he said. <hi type="italic">“Yea, thy servant Joab, he hath commanded me, and he hath put all these words into thy servant’s mouth.”</hi> אשׁ is not a copyist’s error, but a softer form of ישׁ, as in Mic 6:10 (vid., Ewald, §53 <hi type="italic">c</hi>, and Olshausen, <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. p. 425).
entries.0176160fdbae980faa9d219f1c1cc9fa195e9d6f: <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.20">2Sa 14:20</reference> <hi type="italic">“To turn the appearance of the king </hi>(i.e., to disguise the affair in the finest way) <hi type="italic">Joab hath done this; my lord</hi> (i.e., the king),<hi type="italic">however, is wise, like the wisdom of the angel of God, to know all that is </hi>(happens) <hi type="italic">upon earth.”</hi> She hoped by these flattering words to gain the king completely over.
entries.93b7e0851960ad824a52587355c936c984f74b4b: <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.21">2Sa 14:21</reference> <div eID="gen4440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4441" type="x-p"/> David then promised Joab, that the request which he had presented through the medium of the woman of Tekoah should be fulfilled, and commanded him to fetch Absalom back. The <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> עשׂתי (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.21">2Sa 14:21</reference>) is the correct reading, and the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> עשׂית has arisen from a misunderstanding.
entries.44e9d048e6efa1dc2bc8c07ba9f187cef0c59e3b: <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.22">2Sa 14:22</reference> <div eID="gen4441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4442" type="x-p"/> Joab thanked the king for this, and blessed him: <hi type="italic">“To-day thy servant knoweth that I have found grace in thy sight, my lord, O king, in that the king hath fulfilled the request of his servant.”</hi> It is pretty evident from this, that Joab had frequently applied to David for Absalom’s return, without any attention being paid to his application. David therefore suspected that Joab had instructed the woman of Tekoah. The <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> עבדּו is not to be exchanged for the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> עבדּך.
entries.22bc8a3886f58769e845f6ed26c78c1072eeb200: <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.23">2Sa 14:23</reference> <div eID="gen4442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4443" type="x-p"/> Joab then went to <hi type="italic">Geshur</hi> (see <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.37">2Sa 13:37</reference>), and fetched Absalom back to Jerusalem.
entries.613a9123f6e44f2348317ef08c5219a3047aaed6: <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.24">2Sa 14:24</reference> <div eID="gen4443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4444" type="x-p"/> But David could not forgive Absalom altogether. He said to Joab, <hi type="italic">“Let him turn to his own house, and my face he shall not see.”</hi> This half forgiveness was an imprudent measure, and bore very bitter fruit. The further account of Absalom is introduced in <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.25-2Sam.14.27">2Sa 14:25-27</reference> with a description of his personal appearance and family affairs.
entries.7d5cc2a84d04b328d4b23405b74ece21b5b20121: <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.25">2Sa 14:25</reference> <div eID="gen4444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4445" type="x-p"/> There was no man in all Israel so handsome as Absalom. מאד להלּל, “to much praising,” i.e., so that he was greatly praised. from the sole of the foot even to the crown of his head, there was no fault (מוּם, bodily blemish) in him.
entries.2eee885358d5e22387a95542e6fac2dee0cd11c6: <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.26">2Sa 14:26</reference> <hi type="italic">“When he polled his head, and it took place from year to year that he polled it; for it became heavy upon him </hi>(too heavy for him), <hi type="italic">and so he polled it: they weighed the hair of his head, two hundred shekels by the king’s weight.”</hi> A strong growth of hair was a sign of great manly power, and so far a proof of Absalom’s beauty. The statement as to the weight of the hair cut off, viz., two hundred shekels, is in any case a round number, and much too high, although we do not know what the difference between the royal and the sacred shekel really was. According to the sacred reckoning, two hundred shekels would be about six pounds; so that if we were to assume that the royal shekel was about half the other, the number would be still much too high. It is evident, therefore, that there is an error in the text, such as we frequently meet with in the case of numbers, though we have no means of rectifying it, as all the ancient versions contain the same number.
entries.714b5e98ec820b7f2397f08400fbb94e5fcf76bb: <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.27">2Sa 14:27</reference> <div eID="gen4445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4446" type="x-p"/> Unto Absalom there were born three sons, and one daughter named Tamar, who was beautiful in figure. Contrary to general usage, the names of the sons are not given, in all probability for no other reason than because they died in infancy. Consequently, as Absalom had no sons, he afterwards erected a pillar to preserve his name (<reference osisRef="2Sam.18.18">2Sa 18:18</reference>). The daughter’s name is probably given as a proof of Absalom’s great affection for his sister Tamar, whom Amnon had violated.<note placement="foot">The lxx have this additional clause, καὶ γίνεται γυνὴ Ῥοβαὰμ υἱῷ Σαλωμὼν καὶ τίκτει αὐτῷ τὸν Ἀβιά (and she became the wife of Rehoboam the son of Solomon, and bore him a son named Abia). Although this is quite at variance with 1Ki 15:2, where it is stated that the wife of Rehoboam and mother of Abia (Abijam) was named <hi type="italic">Maacah</hi>, the clause had been adopted by Thenius, who regards it as original, though for reasons which Böttcher has shown to be worthless.</note>
entries.11d3e6c712ca3d0e4c3cd2d1265995d51f741b9c: <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.28-2Sam.14.30">2Sa 14:28-30</reference> <div eID="gen4446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4447" type="x-p"/> After Absalom had sat for two whole years in his house at Jerusalem without seeing the king’s face, he sent to Joab that he might obtain for him the king’s full forgiveness. But as Joab would not come to him, even after he had sent for him twice, Absalom commanded his servants to set fire to one of Joab’s fields which adjoined his own and was then full of barley, for the purpose of compelling him to come, as he foresaw that Joab would not take this destruction of his property quietly, but would come to him to complain. ידי אל, literally “at my hand,” i.e., by the side of my field or property. The <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> והוציתה (“come, I will set it on fire”) is a <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> formation, according to verbs ופ, for which the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> has והצּיתוּה, the ordinary <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> form of יצת in the second person plural, “go and set it one fire.”
entries.d46de1389a6b3ac4f097b1bf356f9353a66b2951: <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.31-2Sam.14.33">2Sa 14:31-33</reference> <div eID="gen4447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4448" type="x-p"/> When Joab came to Absalom’s house in consequence of this, and complained of it, Absalom said to him, “See, I have sent to thee, to say to thee, Come hither, and I will send thee to the king, to say to him, Wherefore have I come from Geshur? it were better for me that I were there still: and now I will see the king’s face; and if there is any iniquity in me, let him put me to death.” This half forgiving was really worse than no forgiveness at all. Absalom might indeed very properly desire to be punished according to the law, if the king could not or might not forgive him; although the manner in which he sought to obtain forgiveness by force manifested an evident spirit of defiance, by which, with the well-known mildness of David’s temper, he hoped to attain his object, and in fact did attain it. For (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.33">2Sa 14:33</reference>) when Joab went to the king, and announced this to him, the king sent for Absalom, and kissed him, as a sign of his restoration to favour. Nothing was said by Absalom about forgiveness; for his falling down before the king when he came into his presence, was nothing more than the ordinary manifestation of reverence with which a subject in the East approaches his king. Absalom’s Rebellion and David’s Flight - 2 Samuel 15-16:14 <div eID="gen4448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4449" type="x-p"/> After this restoration to favour, Absalom soon began to aspire to the throne, setting up a princely court, and endeavouring to turn the hearts of the people towards himself, by addressing in a friendly manner any who came to seek redress from the king in matters in dispute, and by saying things adapted to throw suspicion upon his father’s rule (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.1-2Sam.15.6">2Sa 15:1-6</reference>). When he had succeeded in this, he asked permission from the king to take a journey to Hebron, under the pretence of wanting to fulfil a vow which he had made during his banishment; and when once there, he soon proceeded with his rebellious intentions (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.7-2Sam.15.12">2Sa 15:7-12</reference>). As soon as David heard of it, he determined to fly from Jerusalem, and crossed the Kidron with his faithful adherents. Having sent the priests with the ark of the covenant back to the city, he went up to the Mount of Olives, amidst the loud lamentations of the people. Hushai, who came to meet him, he sent to the city, to frustrate the counsel of Ahithophel, who was one of the conspirators, and to send information to him of what was going forward (vv. 13-37). When he reached the top, Ziba, Mephibosheth’s servant, came to meet him with provisions and succour (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.1-2Sam.16.4">2Sa 16:1-4</reference>) whilst Shimei, a relation of the house of Saul, followed him with curses and stones (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5-2Sam.16.14">2Sa 16:5-14</reference>). <div eID="gen4449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4450" type="x-p"/> With this rebellion the calamities which Nathan had predicted to David on account of his sin with Bathsheba began to burst upon him in all their fulness. The success of the rebellion itself may be accounted for, from the fact that the consciousness of his own fault not only made David weak towards his sons, but produced a want of firmness in his resolutions; whilst the imperfections and defects in the internal administration of the kingdom, when the time of the brilliant victories was past, became more and more perceptible to the people, and furnished occasion for dissatisfaction with his government, which Absalom was skilful enough to bend to his own purposes. During the time that this rebellion was in progress, David poured out his lamentations to the Lord (in <reference osisRef="Ps.41.1-Ps.41.13">Psa 41:1-13</reference> and 55) as to the faithlessness of his most confidential councillors, and prayed for the judgment of retribution upon the conduct of this wicked band. After it had broken out, he uttered his longings to return to the sanctuary at Jerusalem, and his firm confidence that he should be delivered out of his distresses and reinstated in his kingdom, first of all in <reference osisRef="Ps.3.1-Ps.3.8">Psa 3:1-8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:1-11</reference> during his flight in the desert of Judah, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.61.1-Ps.61.8">Psa 61:1-8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.62.1-Ps.62.12">Psa 62:1-12</reference> during his stay in the land to the east of the Jordan.  <chapter eID="2Sam.14"/> <div eID="gen4450" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XIV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>NOw Joab the son of Zeruiah, perceived that the kings heart <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> toward Absalom <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">He desired to see him, but was ashamed to show kind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness to one whom Gods Law and his own Conscience obliged him to punish; and wanted a fair pretence, which therefore <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> gave him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And Joab sent to Tekoah <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">A City of <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 11. 5, 6. One of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> was not convenient, lest the King might know the person, or search out the business. And besides, this Woman seems to be of great eminency for her Wisdom, as the following dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />course manifests.</ns0:note>, and fetcht thence a wise woman <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Rather than a <ns0:hi>Man,</ns0:hi> because Women can more easily express their passions, and do sooner pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cure pity in their miseries, and an answer to their requests.</ns0:note>, and said unto her, I pray thee, feign thy self to be a mourner, and put on now mourning apparel, and anoint not thy self with oil <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">As they used to do when they were out of a Mourning state. See <ns0:hi>Ruth</ns0:hi> 3. 3. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 6. 17.</ns0:note>, but be as a woman that had a long time mourned for the dead:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And come to the king, and speak on this manner unto him: so Joab put the words in her mouth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 ¶ And when the woman of Tekoah spake to the king, she fell on her face to the ground, and did obeisance, and said, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> save.</ns0:note> Help, O king.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And the king said unto her, What aileth thee? And she answered, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> indeed a widow-woman <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">One of them who most need thy compassion and assistance, and whom thou art by Gods Law obliged in a singular manner to protect and relieve.</ns0:note>, and mine husband is dead.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And thy handmaid had two sons, and they two strove together in the field, and <ns0:hi>there was</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> no de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liverer be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tween them.</ns0:note> none to part them <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">And therefore there is no witness, either that he killed him, or how he killed him, whether from some sudden pas<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion and great provocation, or in his own necessary defence, or otherwise.</ns0:note>, but the one smote the other, and slew him <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">As the avengers of Blood report.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:258" rendition="simple:additions" />7 And behold, the whole family is risen against thine handmaid, and they said, Deliver him that smote his brother, that we may kill him <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">According to the Law, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 35. 19. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 19. 12.</ns0:note>, for the life of his brother whom he slew, and we will de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroy the heir also <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">So they plainly discover, that their prosecution of him was not so much from love of Justice, as from a covetous desire to deprive him of the Inheritance, and to transfer it to them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves; which self-interest might justly render their Testi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mony suspected. Or, perhaps these words are not spoken as the express words of the prosecutors (who can hardly be thought so directly to express a sinister design) as the Wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mans Inference or Comment upon what they were doing: (for this would be indeed the result of it, though they did not so in express words) thereby to lie to represent her case as the more deserving pity.</ns0:note>: and so they shall quench my coal which is left <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The poor remainder of my light and comfort, by whom alone my hopes may be revived and repaired.</ns0:note>, and shall not leave to my husband <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">She names him rather than her self, because Children bear the names of their Fathers, not of their Mothers.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>neither</ns0:hi> name nor remainder <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> upon the face of the earth.</ns0:note> upon the earth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And the king said unto the woman, Go to thine house, and I will give charge concerning thee <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">That thy cause may be justly and truly examined, and thy Son preserved from their unjust and malicious pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceedings.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And the woman of Tekoah said unto the king, My lord, O king, the iniquity <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> on me, and on my fathers house: and the king and his throne <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> guiltless <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">The sense is, either, first, this, If I do not inform thee aright, and thou thereby beest drawn to give an unrighteous sentence on my behalf, I am willing to bear the whole blame of it before God and Men; I acknowledge thou art wholly innocent in the case. Compare <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 27. 13. Or, Secondly, this, If through thy forgetfulness or neg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lect of this my just cause, my adversaries prevail and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroy my Son, my desire is, that God would not lay it to the Kings charge, but rather to me and mine, so the King may be exempted thereby. Whereby she both insinuates her great e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />steem of, and affection for the King, thereby winning upon him to compass her design; and withal implies, that such an omis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion of the Kings will bring guilt upon him; and yet most prudently and decently orders her Phrase so as not to seem to blame or threaten the King. Compare <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 5. 16. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 20. 16. This sense seems best to agree with <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s answer, which shews that she desired some further assurance of the Kings care and justice in her concern.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And the king said, Whosoever saith <ns0:hi>ought</ns0:hi> unto thee<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> bring him to me, and he shall not touch thee <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> So as to hurt or molest thee, by pursuing thy Son.</ns0:note> any more.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Then said she, I pray thee, let the king re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />member the LORD thy God <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The sense is, either, first, Make mention (as this <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Verb is oft rendred) of the name of the Lord thy God, to wit, in an Oath; <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Swear to me by God, That thou wilt protect me and my Son against the revenger of Blood. For so <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> did in compliance with this desire of hers. Onely she was forced to express her mind in more general and am<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />biguous terms, because it had been presumption and rude<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness for her in plain terms to desire the Kings Oath, as if she durst not trust his word; yet withal she insinuates her mean<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing so plainly, that the King understood it; and yet so hand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />somly and elegantly, that the King was much pleased with her Wisdom, and thereby inclined to grant her request. Or, Secondly, this, Remember the Gracious nature of thy God, who is not too severe and rigorous to mark at all that is amiss, nor doth cut off every manslayer, as appears from <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 35. and from the example of <ns0:hi>Cain,</ns0:hi> and from thy self, O King: though this she expresseth not, but onely useth such words which <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                        </ns0:gap>he knew would give so wise and good a King occasion to reflect upon himself and upon the good<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of God in sparing him, though a wilful Murtherer, that thereby he might be obliged to imitate God, in sparing the person whom she designed. Or, Thirdly, this, Remember the Lord, in whose presence thou hast made me this pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mise, and who will be a witness against thee, if thou break<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est it.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> that the revenger of blood do not multiply to destroy</ns0:note> that thou wouldest not suffer the revengers of blood to destroy any more <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>lest the avenger of blood multiply to destroy, i. e.</ns0:hi> lest they cause one destruction to another, and add my surviving Son to him who is slain already. Or, <ns0:hi>lest thou dost multiply avengers of blood to destroy, i. e.</ns0:hi> lest by thy connivence at their cruel and malicious proceedings against my Son, thou dost encourage avengers of Blood to the like furious practices, and thereby increase the number of that sort of Men, and upon that pretence occasion multitudes of Murthers.</ns0:note>, lest they destroy my son <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>and let them not destroy my Son;</ns0:hi> the Fu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture Tense, being put for the Imperative Mood, as is fre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quent.</ns0:note>.                   <ns0:p n="12">12 Then the woman said <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Having obliged the King by his Oath in her supposed case, she now throws off the vail, and begins to apply this parable to the Kings and Kingdoms present case.</ns0:note>, Let thine handmaid, I pray thee, speak <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> word unto my lord the king. And he said, Say on:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And the woman said, Wherefore then hast thou thought such a thing against the people of God <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">If thou wouldst not permit the avengers of Blood to molest me, or to destroy my Son, who are but two persons; how unreasonable is it that thou shouldst proceed in thy in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deavours to avenge <ns0:hi>Amnon</ns0:hi>'s blood upon <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> whose death would be highly injurious and grievous to the whole Commonwealth of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> all whose eyes are upon him as the Heir of the Crown, and a wise, and valiant, and amiable person, unhappy onely in this one act of killing <ns0:hi>Amnon,</ns0:hi> which was done upon an high and hainous provocation, and whereof thou thy self didst give the occasion by permitting <ns0:hi>Amnon</ns0:hi> to go unpunished?</ns0:note>? for the king doth speak this thing as one which is faulty <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">By thy Word, and Promise, and Oath given to me for my Son, thou condemnest thy self for not allowing the same equity towards thy own Son.</ns0:note>, in that the king doth not fetch home again his banished <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">To wit, <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> from that Heathenish Countrey where he is in evident danger of being infected with their Idolatry and other vices: which is likely to be a great and pub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lick mischief to all thy people, if he come to Reign in thy stead, which he is very likely to do. It is true, there was a considerable disparity between her Sons, and <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s case, the one being a rash and sudden action, the other a deliberate and premeditated Murther; but that may seem to be balanced in some measure; partly, by <ns0:hi>Amnon</ns0:hi>'s great and lasting provocation; and principally, by the vast difference between a private injury, which was her case, and a publick calamity and grievance, which she affirmed, and the King easily believed was <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s case: And what <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi> said in the case of <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi>'s Murther of <ns0:hi>Abner,</ns0:hi> That he could not revenge it, because <ns0:hi>the sons of Zeruiah were too hard for him,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 3. 39. the like peradventure might have been said in this case, where the Peoples hearts may seem to have been universally and vehemently set upon <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> and the rather, because his long banishment moved their pity, and his absence made him more desirable, as it frequently happens among people; and therefore it might really be out of the Kings power to punish him; and so he might seem to be obliged to spare him for the common safety of his whole Kingdom.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 For we must needs die <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>In dying we shall die,</ns0:hi> i. e. we shall certainly and suddenly die all of us, both thou, O King, who therefore art obliged to take due care of thy Successor, who is <ns0:hi>Absa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lom;</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> who, if he do not die by the hand of Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stice, must shortly die by the necessity of Nature: and <ns0:hi>Am<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />non</ns0:hi> too must have died in the common way of all flesh, if <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> had not cut him off.                               <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> neither doth God respect <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> person <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To wit, so far as to exempt him from this common Law of dying. But this version seems not to agree with the Scripture Phrase: for the <ns0:hi>accepting of a person</ns0:hi> is never to my knowledge ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressed in <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Nasa Nephesh,</ns0:hi> which is the Phrase here, but by <ns0:hi>Nasa Panim,</ns0:hi> every where. The words therefore may be rendred either thus: <ns0:hi>yet God will not take away,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>doth not use to take away</ns0:hi> (the Future Tense oft noting a continued act, as <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                        </ns0:hi> observe) <ns0:hi>the soul,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>souls,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>lives</ns0:hi> of men, to wit, by violence. God doth not severely and instantly cut off offenders, but suffers them to live till they die by the course of Nature; and therefore so shouldst thou do too. Or, rather thus: <ns0:hi>yet God hath not taken away</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>soul</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>life,</ns0:hi> the Pronoun, <ns0:hi>his,</ns0:hi> being understood here, as it is in many other places, and as being easily supplied out of the context. So the sense is, God hath hitherto spared him, and did not suffer his Brethren to kill him, as in reason might have been expected; nor hath God himself yet cut him off for his Murther, as he oft doth with persons who are out of the Magistrates reach; but hath hitherto pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />served him even in a Heathenish Land. All which are inti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mations that God would have him spared.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>yet</ns0:hi> doth he devise means, that his banished be not expelled from him <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>but hath devised means,</ns0:hi> &c. i. e. hath given Laws to this purpose, That the manslayer who is banished should not always con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinue in banishment, but upon the High-Priests death return to his own City. Whereby he hath shewed his pleasure, that the avenger of Blood should not implacably persist in seek<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing revenge, and that the manslayer should be spared. Or rather, thus, <ns0:hi>but thinketh thoughts,</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>but hath designed,</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>therefore he intendeth that he who is banished</ns0:hi> (to wit, <ns0:hi>Ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salom) be not</ns0:hi> (always) <ns0:hi>expelled</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>banished from him,</ns0:hi> i. e. from God and from his People, and from the place of his Worship, but that he should return home to him. So the sense is, That God by sparing <ns0:hi>Absaloms</ns0:hi> life in the midst of dangers, did sufficiently intimate, that he would in due time bring him back to his Land and People. Even as in our Days and Land, Gods miraculous preservation of the Life of our present Sovereign in so many and great dangers, was a pledge and presage that God intended sooner or later to re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />store him to his Kingdoms.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:258" />15 Now therefore that I am come to speak of this thing unto my lord the king, <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> because the people have made me afraid <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The truth is, I was even forced to this bold Address to thee, by the disposition and condition of thy people, who are discontented at <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s perpetual banishment, and full of fears; either lest, upon thy death, which none knoweth how soon it may happen, they should be involved in a Civil War about thy Successor; or lest, in the mean time, if <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> by his Father-in-laws assistance invade the Land, and indea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vour by force to regain and secure his right to the Successi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, the people, who have a great opinion of him, and kind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness for him, and think he is very hardly used, should take up Arms for him; or lest he who is thy Heir and Succes<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sor should by continual and familiar conversation with Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thens, be insnared in their Errors, or alienated from the true Religion, and from Gods Worship, from which he is now ut<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />terly excluded.</ns0:note>: and thy handmaid said <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>therefore thy handmaid said,</ns0:hi> either, within my self, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I intended: or, to the people, to quiet them.</ns0:note>, I will now speak unto the king; it may be that the king will perform the request of his hand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />maid.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 For the king will hear <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">For I know the King is so wise and just, that I assure my self of Audience and Acceptation. Which expectation of hers is cunningly insinuated here, that the King might conceive himself obliged to answer it, and not to disappoint her hope, nor to forfeit that good opinion which his Subjects now had of him.</ns0:note>, to deliver his hand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />maid out of the hand of the man <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To grant my request concerning my Son, and consequently the peoples Petition concerning <ns0:hi>Ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salom.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>that would</ns0:hi> de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroy me and my son <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Implying that her life was bound up in the life of her Son, and that she could not out-live his death; (and supposing, it is like, that it might be <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s case also, and would therefore touch him in a tender part, though it were not proper to say it expresly): and thereby suggesting, that the tranquillity, safety, and comfort of the people of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> depended upon <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s Restitution, and the settle<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of the Succession in him.</ns0:note> together out of the inhe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritance of God <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Out of that Inheri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tance which God hath given to me and mine: or, out of that Land which God gave to his people to be their Inhe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritance and Possession, and in which alone God hath settled the place of his Presence and Worship. Whereby she inti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mates the danger of <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s living in a state of separation from God, and his House, and amongst Idolaters.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 Then thine handmaid said, The word of my lord the king shall now be <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> for rest.</ns0:note> comfortable <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">I doubt not the King will give a gracious and satisfacto<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry Answer to my Pe<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>tion.</ns0:note>: for as an angel of God <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To wit, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> Wisdom, and Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stice, and Goodness.</ns0:note>, so <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my lord the king <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to hear.</ns0:note> to dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cern good and bad <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">To hear and judge of Causes and Requests, whether they be just, and good, and fit to be granted, as mine is; or unrighteous, and unreasonable, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> fit to be rejected. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> confidence in the Justice of her Cause, and thereby confirms the King in his purpose and promise to grant her Request, and withal arms the King against the suggestions of them who should advise him to a rigorous execution of Gods Law against <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> and be ready to censure him for restoring <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> and this for want of that Angelical Wisdom which the King had, who wisely considered many things far above their reach.</ns0:note>: therefore <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Because thou art so wise, and just, and pitiful, and graci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous to those who in strict Justice deserve punishment.</ns0:note> the LORD thy God will be with thee <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">God will own and stand by thee in this thy act of Grace: or, God will prosper thee in thy enterprizes: or, at least, not be offended with thee.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 Then the king answered and said unto the woman, Hide not from me, I pray thee, the thing that I shall ask thee. And the woman said, Let my lord the king now speak.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And the king said, <ns0:hi>Is not</ns0:hi> the hand of Joab with thee in all this <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Hast thou not said and done this by <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi>'s direction and contrivance?</ns0:note>? And the woman answered, and said, <ns0:hi>As</ns0:hi> thy soul liveth, my lord the king, none can turn to the right hand, or to the left, from ought that my lord the king hath spoken <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">As the King is so wise that no man can deceive him by any turnings or windings to the right or left hand, but he quickly searcheth out the truth in every thing; so (it is a folly to dissemble, or go about to conceal it) it is even so, thou hast now discovered the truth of this business.</ns0:note>: for thy servant Joab he bade me, and he put all these words in the mouth of thine handmaid <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">To wit, for the scope and substance of them, but not as to all the expressions which she used, for these were to be varied as the Kings answer gave occasion, which also she did with singular prudence.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 To fetch about this form of speech <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To propose mine, and his, and the peoples desire of <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s restitution in this parabolical manner, in mine, and my Sons person.</ns0:note> hath thy servant Joab done this thing: and my lord <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> wise, according to the wisdom of an angel of God, to know all <ns0:hi>things</ns0:hi> that <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> in the earth <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>in this Land,</ns0:hi> in all thy King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom; all the counsels and devices of thy Subjects, which have any relation to thee or thy affairs.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 ¶ And the king said unto Joab, Behold now, I have done this thing <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">In compliance with thy desire: although in truth it was according to his own desire. He overlooks the Woman in this grant, because she was but <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi>'s Instrument in it.</ns0:note>: go therefore, bring the young man <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">By which expression he mitigates his Crime, as being an act of youthful heat, and folly, and rashness.</ns0:note> Absalom again.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And Joab fell to the ground on his face, and bowed himself, and <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> blessed.</ns0:note> thanked the king: and Jo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ab said, To day thy servant knoweth that I have found grace in thy sight, my lord, O king, in that the king hath fulfilled the request of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> thy.</ns0:note> his servant <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Restored <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> at my request. Whereby <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> thought to establish himself for ever, and that he should be both the Fathers and the Sons favourite. <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> Whether <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> did well in granting this request? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Although there be some circumstances which in part extenuate <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s fault herein, as <ns0:hi>Amnon</ns0:hi>'s high provocation of <ns0:hi>Absalom; Ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salom</ns0:hi>'s being out of the reach of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Justice, where al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />so he could and would have kept himself, if <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had not promised him impunity; the extream danger of <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s infection by Heathenish principles and practises; the safety of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Kingdom, which seemed to depend upon the Establishment of the Succession, and that upon <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> to whom the hearts of the people were so universally and ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hemently inclined, if the matter was really so, and not pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tended or magnified by the art of this subtil Woman; yet it seems most probable that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was faulty herein, because this action was directly contrary to the express Laws of God, which strictly command the Supreme Magistrate to execute Justice upon all wilful Murtherers, without any reservation, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 9. 6. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 35. 30, 31. And <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had no power to dispence with Gods Laws, nor to spare any whom God com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />manded him to destroy: for the Laws of God did bind the Kings and Rulers, as well as the people of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> to observe and obey them, as is most evident from <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 17. 18, 19. and from <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 1. 8. and many other places. And indeed we may read <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s sin in the Glass of those tremendous Judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments of God which befel him, by means of his indulgence to <ns0:hi>Absalom.</ns0:hi> For although Gods Providences be in themselves no Rule to Judge of the good or evil of Mens actions; yet where they comply with Gods word, and accomplish his threatnings, as here they did, they are to be taken for the tokens of Gods displeasure.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:259" />23 So Joab arose and went to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And the king said, Let him turn to his own house, and let him not see my face <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Lest whilst he shewed some mercy to <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> he should seem to approve of his sin, and thereby wound his own conscience, and lose his honour, and encourage him and others to such like attempts; and that by this means <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> might be drawn to a more thorough humiliation and true repentance.</ns0:note>. So Absalom returned to his own house, and saw not the kings face.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 ¶ <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> and as Absalom there was not a beautiful man in all Israel to praise greatly.</ns0:note> But in all Israel there was none to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">This is here noted as the occasion of his pride and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />solency, and of the peoples affections to him, and conse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quently of the following Rebellion.</ns0:note>: from the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head, there was no blemish in him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And when he polled his head, (for it was at every years end that he polled it: because <ns0:hi>the hair</ns0:hi> was heavy on him, therefore he polled it) he weighed the hair of his head at two hundred shekels <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Whereas ordinarily the hair of a Manss head which grows in a years space, comes not to half so much. But some Mens hair grows much faster, and is much heavier than others. But others understand this not of the weight, but of the price of his hair, which was sold by him that Polled it at that rate.</ns0:note>, after the kings <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> stone.</ns0:note> weight.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And unto Absalom there were born three sons <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">All which died not long after they were born, as may be gathered from <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 18. 18. where it is said, that <ns0:hi>Absalom had no son.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> and one daughter, whose name <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> Tamar <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">So called from her Aunt, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 13. 1.</ns0:note>: she was a woman of a fair countenance.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 ¶ So Absalom dwelt two full years in Je<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rusalem, and saw not the kings face.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 Therefore Absalom sent for Joab, to have sent him to the king <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">That by his mediation he might be admitted into the Kings favour and presence.</ns0:note>, but he would not come to him: and when he sent again the second time, he would not come <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Partly, because perceiving <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s affections to be cold to <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> he would not ven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture his own Interest for him, especially in desiring that which he feared he should be denied; partly, lest by inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceeding further for <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> he should revive the remem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brance of his former Murther, and meet with the reproach of one Murtherers interceeding for another; and partly, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause by converse with <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> he observed his temper to be such, that if once he were fully restored to the Kings fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vour, he would not onely eclipse and oppose <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi>'s interest and power with the King, but also attempt high things, not without danger to the King and Kingdom, as it happened.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 Therefore he said unto his servants, See, Jo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />abs field is <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> near my place.</ns0:note> near mine, and he hath barley there; go and set it on fire <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">That <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> may be forced to come to me to complain of, and demand reparations for this injury.</ns0:note>: and Absaloms servants set the field on fire.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 Then Joab arose and came to Absalom unto <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> house, and said unto him, Wherefore have thy servants set my field on fire?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 And Absalom answered Joab, Behold, I sent unto thee, saying, Come hither that I may send thee to the king, to say, Wherefore am I come from Geshur? <ns0:hi>It had been</ns0:hi> good for me <ns0:hi>to have been</ns0:hi> there still <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Rather than here, because my estrangement from him now when I am so near to him, is both more grievous and more shameful to me. But the truth of the business was this, <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> saw that his Father had accomplished his design in bringing him thither, having satisfied both his own Natural affection, and his peoples desire of <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s return from banishment; but that he could not without restitution into the Kings presence and favour compass his design, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />firm and improve that interest which he saw he had in the peoples hearts.</ns0:note>: now therefore let me see the kings face: and if there be <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> iniquity in me, let him kill me <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">For it is better for me to die, than to want the sight and favour of my dear Father. Thus he in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sinuates himself into his Fathers affections, by pretending such Respect and Love to him. It seems that by this time <ns0:hi>Ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salom</ns0:hi> having so far recovered his Fathers favour, as to be re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />called, he began to grow upon him, and take so much confi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence as to stand upon his own justification, as if what he had done, had been no iniquity, at least not such as to deserve death. For so much this speech intimates.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 So Joab came to the king, and told him: and when he had called for Absalom, he came to the king, and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king: and the king kissed Ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salom <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">In testimony of his thorough Reconciliation to him. Which <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> did very ill requite, as the next Chapter manifesteth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
